questions.q: What is the formal condition for a matrix U to be unitary, and what does it mean physically for a quantum gate?
options: U @ U.conj().T must equal the identity matrix I; physically, this guarantees the gate preserves a state's total probability (norm)
U must equal its own transpose without conjugation, U == U.T
U must have a determinant of exactly 0
U must contain only real numbers, with no imaginary entries allowed anywhere
questions.explain: Unitary means U @ U.conj().T == I. Physically this is why every valid quantum gate must be unitary -- it guarantees applying the gate never creates or destroys total measurement probability.

questions.q: The lesson shows that Pauli-Y is both unitary and Hermitian, while the S-gate (diag(1, j)) is unitary but not Hermitian. What does this pair of examples prove?
options: Unitary and Hermitian are independent properties -- a matrix can satisfy one, both, or neither, with no implication between them
Hermitian matrices are a subset of unitary matrices with no exceptions
Every unitary matrix must also be Hermitian, and the S-gate result was a calculation error
Pauli-Y and the S-gate are actually the same matrix written two different ways
questions.explain: Pauli-Y satisfies both U@U.conj().T==I and A==A.conj().T, while S satisfies only the first. This direct side-by-side comparison proves the two properties don't imply each other.

questions.q: For the S-gate S = diag(1, j), computing S @ S_dagger gives the identity matrix, but np.array_equal(S, S_dagger) returns False. What specifically differs between S and S_dagger?
options: S_dagger has an extra row that S does not have
S and S_dagger have different shapes, so they cannot be compared at all
There is no real difference; np.array_equal simply has a bug with complex numbers
The bottom-right entry: S has j there while S_dagger has -j, so the matrices are not element-wise equal even though S is still unitary
questions.explain: Conjugating S flips the sign of its only imaginary entry, turning the bottom-right j into -j. S @ S_dagger still equals I (confirming unitarity), but S itself does not equal S_dagger (confirming it is not Hermitian).

questions.q: The lesson defines `is_unitary` and `is_hermitian` using `np.allclose` rather than Python's `==` operator. Based on how the lesson frames this choice, why is that the more robust approach?
options: np.allclose is simply faster to type and has no functional difference from ==
== only works on integers, never on arrays containing complex numbers
np.allclose is required because Python's == operator cannot be used on NumPy arrays under any circumstances
Floating-point computations rarely land on an exact value, so an approximate comparison with a tolerance avoids false negatives from tiny rounding error
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly ties this choice to floating-point rounding (explored fully in Lesson 12) -- exact equality would reject a genuinely unitary or Hermitian matrix just because of a tiny rounding artifact in the computed product.

questions.q: Applying Y to the state psi = (|0> + j|1>)/sqrt(2) returns psi unchanged (Y @ psi == psi exactly). What does this specific result demonstrate about psi and about unitary gates in general?
options: This proves Y is not unitary, since a unitary gate should always change the input vector
psi must have been entered incorrectly, since applying any gate should always produce a different vector
psi is an eigenvector of Y with eigenvalue +1, and more generally, a unitary gate applied to a normalized state always yields another state with the same total norm
Y failed to do anything to the state, which means Y is not actually a valid quantum gate
questions.explain: Y @ psi reproducing psi exactly means psi is an eigenvector of Y with eigenvalue +1 -- a real, valid outcome. More generally, because Y is unitary, applying it to any normalized state (whether or not it's an eigenvector) always preserves the state's norm.
